Beddor and Goldstein offer a motivational story on which retraction is no longer standing by the update associated with an earlier modal assertion (PDF page 2, section 1) [lit:eps2-L3:E1].

They reject a modal-knowledge ascription using assessor information (PDF page 9, section 3.3, footnote 12) [lit:eps2-L3:E2], and they state the safety condition separately from truth at an information index (PDF pages 17 and 23–24, sections 5.2–5.4) [lit:eps2-L3:E3].

They also allow that contextual probability may model an assessor's provisionally revised credences, without identifying or deriving assessment-sensitive retraction (PDF pages 27–30, sections 6.2–6.3) [lit:eps2-L3:E4].

Dinges explains retraction of knowledge ascriptions through stakes-dependent estimates of epistemic qualities, extendable to safety or reliability, consistently with denying relativism; this is a rival behavioural bridge and not a worldly-information semantics (PDF pages 3–6 and 10–11, section 4.3.1 and footnote 10) [lit:eps2-L3:E6].

Holliday and Mandelkern cite Beddor and Goldstein on modal knowledge but leave the pragmatics of truth, correctness, agreement and retraction to further development (PDF pages 55 and 58) [lit:eps2-L3:E7].
